title: Mean Reversion
tagline: RSI, Bollinger bands, pairs spreads and short-horizon reversal, and the regimes that break them
summary: Mean reversion bets that a move overshoots and then gives some of itself back. This course separates that hypothesis from trend, builds RSI and Bollinger rules, constructs a pairs spread by a ratio and by a hedge ratio, and treats cross-sectional reversal as the same idea applied to a ranking. The last chapter is about failure: a reversion rule in a trend, and an exit rule that dominates the entry.
overview: Short-horizon equity returns have, in several classic studies, tended to reverse: last month’s losers have outperformed last month’s winners over the next month, before costs. That sentence is not a trading rule. A trading rule names the universe, the horizon, the entry, the exit and the cost. RSI thresholds, a close below a Bollinger band, and a z-score of a log price ratio are three such namings. They can all lose money in a sample where the historical average reversal was positive, because the implementation is part of the hypothesis.

Pairs trading tightens the idea. Two prices that share a common component may leave a spread that is more stable than either price. A ratio z-score and a rolling ordinary-least-squares hedge ratio are different estimates of that spread. Neither is cointegration until the assumptions of a cointegration test are stated and checked. The course states them and does not pretend a single z-score plot is the test.

The open library includes both profitable-looking and loss-making reversion examples, including a trailing-stop exit on an RSI entry whose reported compound return is negative. Those pages are there to be read, not to be ranked into a portfolio. The failure chapter asks which part of the rule broke.
As elsewhere, nothing is a suggestion to trade a pair, a band or an oscillator.
outcomes: State short-horizon reversal as a hypothesis, separate from time-series momentum, and name the horizon each one uses.
Compute Wilder’s RSI and a Bollinger band, and write an entry and an exit in terms of each.
Build a spread as a log price ratio and as a rolling hedge-ratio residual, and state what a z-score assumes.
Distinguish correlation from cointegration and list the assumptions of an Engle–Granger style residual test.
Define a cross-sectional reversal book as a ranking of recent returns with explicit long and short legs.
Diagnose a reversion rule whose exit, rather than its entry, accounts for the reported loss.

history.title: The relative strength index
history.detail: Wilder defined the RSI in New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, as a normalised comparison of average gains and average losses over a fixed window. The 14-period window used everywhere since is his suggestion, not a theorem.

history.title: Mean reversion in stock prices
history.detail: Poterba and Summers reported evidence that stock-price innovations reverse in part over long horizons. The horizon is years, not the few days of an oscillator rule.

history.title: Short-horizon reversal
history.detail: Jegadeesh, and separately Lehmann, documented negative autocorrelation in individual US stock returns at horizons of a week to a month.

history.title: Bollinger bands in print
history.detail: John Bollinger’s book set out the band construction he had used since the early 1980s: a moving average plus and minus a multiple of a moving standard deviation.

history.title: Pairs trading as a relative-value rule
history.detail: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst specified a distance-based pairs rule on US stocks and reported its historical performance after a delay that limits look-ahead in the matching step.
